title: What time is it? — and a pleasant surprise
goal: Tell the time, the days and the parts of the day — and discover that Hungarian reads the half hour in a way that is the opposite of what English speakers expect, so it is worth learning on purpose.
bekal: say when something happens with the ending *-kor*
name the days of the week with their "on that day" forms

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Mikor kezdődik a film?
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon at a bus stop. Budi and Anna are planning to see a film at the Toldi mozi.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me, what time is it?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Because the film starts at seven.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Akkor még van idő. A mozi közel van.
lines.id: Then there's still time. The cinema is close.
lines.literal: then still is time. the cinema near is.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: When does the next bus come?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: In ten minutes, at a quarter to seven.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jó. Akkor hét óra előtt ott vagyunk.
lines.id: Good. Then we'll be there before seven.
lines.literal: good. then seven hour before there we-are.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: Why? Are you getting up early tomorrow?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Igen, hatkor. Nyolckor kezdődik a munkám.
lines.id: Yes, at six. My work starts at eight.
lines.literal: yes, six-at. eight-at it-starts the work-my.

notes: **Fél hét means 6:30, not 7:30 — a trap for English speakers.** Hungarian counts the half hour **toward the next hour**: *fél hét* is "half (the way) to seven". In English, "half seven" is heard by many people as 7:30, so your instinct will pull you the wrong way. Train yourself on purpose: whenever you hear *fél*, subtract from the next hour.

**Negyed and háromnegyed follow the same logic.** *Negyed hét* = 6:15 (a quarter of the way to seven), *háromnegyed hét* = 6:45 (three quarters of the way). English has no equivalent, but once *fél* feels natural, these two come along with it.

**Hétkor, nyolckor, hatkor.** The ending *-kor* means "at (that hour)". It is one of the few Hungarian endings that **does not obey vowel harmony** — it is always *-kor*, whatever the vowels of the base word. Enjoy it; this language rarely hands out such small gifts.

**Two different time questions.** *Hány óra van?* asks what time it is **now**. *Hánykor?* or *Mikor?* asks **when** something happens. Mixing them up is the beginner mistake that most often produces confusing answers.
**Tíz perc múlva** literally means "ten minutes passing" — it means "in ten minutes". Its lookalike *tíz perce* means "ten minutes ago". Two similar words, two opposite directions in time.
**Mert answers miért.** The two share a root, which makes life easy: *Miért?* (why) is answered with *Mert…* (because). Don't confuse *mert* with *mint* (as, than).

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Hungarian divides the hour into quarters and counts forward to the next hour. The table uses seven o'clock as its example.
after: **For official schedules, Hungarians use the long form**: *tizennyolc óra harminc perc* (18:30) at stations, airports and on television. The *fél hét* way is used in everyday conversation.

**Morning and evening are told apart with words, not numbers.** *reggel hétkor* (seven in the morning), *este hétkor* (seven in the evening). Everyday Hungarian uses the 12-hour clock, just like English.

grammars.title: When? The ending -kor and its relatives
body: The time of an event is marked with an ending, just as place is.
after: *Előtt* and *után* are *névutó* — postpositions that stand on their own, like *mellett* in Unit 4. The noun stays bare.
The pair *-tól … -ig* covers a whole stretch: *kilenctől ötig dolgozom* = I work from nine to five. You will use this pattern often when describing a working day in Unit 10.

grammars.title: Days of the week
body: Look at the last row — it is the only one that takes no ending at all.
after: *Hétfő* literally means "head of the week" — and since *hét* means both seven and week, the name makes sense twice. *Vasárnap* means "market day", and because it already contains the word *nap* (day), it needs no ending.
*Hétvége* means weekend — literally "end of the week". "On the weekend" is *hétvégén*.

sections.title: Parts of the day and time words

blocks.text: Notice that *délelőtt* and *délután* are built from *dél* (noon) plus *előtt* and *után* — "before noon" and "after noon". Hungarian likes to build long words out of pieces you already know, and once you notice this, the vocabulary stops feeling foreign.
Month names are very close to English, so there is nothing to memorize — just watch the spelling: *március* with **c** read as *ts*, and *augusztus* with **sz** read as *s*.

Dates are written from big to small, like an address: **2026. augusztus 24.** Read it as *kétezer-huszonhat augusztus huszonnegyedike*. Note that the day uses an ordinal number ending in *-e*: *elseje* (the 1st), *másodika* (the 2nd), *huszonnegyedike* (the 24th).
